misconceptions.description: Believing that strong adjectives (hard-working, passionate, detail-oriented) count as evidence on a resume
misconceptions.trigger: learner fills a bullet with personality adjectives but no action, number, or scope
misconceptions.feedback: Adjectives describe you; evidence shows what you did. Replace "hard-working volunteer" with a verb, a number, and a scope a reader can check.

misconceptions.description: Claiming team or whole-organization outcomes as if they were the student's solo work
misconceptions.trigger: learner writes "built the entire" or "single-handedly" for work that was shared
misconceptions.feedback: State exactly your part. "Wrote the copy for a five-page team site" is more credible than "built the entire web presence."

misconceptions.description: Pasting AI-generated percentages or achievements that the student cannot defend in an interview
misconceptions.trigger: learner keeps an AI-suggested metric with no source in their actual experience
misconceptions.feedback: If you cannot defend a number when a recruiter asks "how did you measure that?", reject it and write a truthful claim instead.

misconceptions.description: Changing the wording of a bullet without adding an action or measurable result
misconceptions.trigger: learner submits a before-after pair where both versions are equally vague
misconceptions.feedback: Revision means new information, not new synonyms. Add what you did and how much, not just a different phrasing of "responsible for."

misconceptions.description: Believing that omitting or softening a real, defensible achievement is more honest or humble than stating it.
misconceptions.trigger: learner deletes or hedges a truthful quantified accomplishment because it sounds like bragging
misconceptions.feedback: The standard is truthful and specific, not quiet. If you can defend the fact against a reference check, state it plainly with its number and scope; hiding a real result is not honesty, it is lost evidence.
